chapter: Boyhood scene: halls and dance music
title: A cornetist grandfather's living as coachman
summary: A cornet-playing relative loved brass music but made his living driving for undertakers and as a drayman.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: What album did your grandfather play out of? Is it all ballgreens? What do you play?

There's another one, originally played cornet. Doctor advised him to get off, and I doubted him he was a hot man. He seemed to have a little, they always chuckle when they speak of hot man, you know. He could send a knife for us as the greatest trumpet player ever lived. In a musical sense, you know. Remember, he used to laugh at trumpet players how they'd lift their horns. They didn't have the right amateur, you know. But he lived for a brass man. It was a school and a cult in itself. A lot of those guys just loved that music. They were in fun of it. Just played for those. I don't know if the money wasn't too much.
Did he make a living plan for him?
No, it was hard to make a living. He worked as a coachman for Undertakers. Later on, he got a team of horses and he worked as a dreamer, an independent dreamer.
I don't see how he worked. Did he get off and play these funerals and everything? That's right.

Yeah, because Undertakers would always have extra drivers, you know. Probably got just as much driving at a funeral as you got for playing in the brass man. Two dollars or three dollars or four dollars. Didn't make much difference. Yeah, there was quite a town. The spirit is still there. Tim, they still get out. Yeah. What was that? Yeah.
